questions.enonce_markdown: An elastic string $AB$, of natural length $1\ \mathrm{m}$, has a particle of mass $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ attached to the end $B$ and the end $A$ is attached to a fixed point. When the system is in equilibrium with $B$ hanging vertically below $A$, the length of the loaded string is $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate the work that must be done in stretching the loaded string from a length of $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ to a length of $1.75\ \mathrm{m}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Constant.** The paper does not print a value of $g$ for this question, so $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is used (with $g = 10$ the answer would be $15.6\ \mathrm{J}$).

**Modulus of elasticity from the equilibrium position.** Natural length $l = 1\ \mathrm{m}$; in equilibrium the length is $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$, so the extension is $x_0 = 0.2\ \mathrm{m}$. The particle hangs at rest, so the tension balances the weight:

$$T_0 = mg = 2\times 9.8 = 19.6\ \mathrm{N}$$

Hooke's law, $T = \dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$:

$$19.6 = \frac{\lambda\times 0.2}{1}\;\Longrightarrow\;\lambda = 98\ \mathrm{N}$$

**Work done in stretching.** The tension at extension $x$ is $T = \dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$, so the work done against the tension when the extension changes from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is

$$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{\lambda x}{l}\,dx = \frac{\lambda}{2l}\left(x_2^2 - x_1^2\right)$$

Lengths $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ and $1.75\ \mathrm{m}$ correspond to extensions $x_1 = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ and $x_2 = 0.75\ \mathrm{m}$:

$$W = \frac{98}{2\times 1}\left(0.75^2 - 0.5^2\right) = 49\,(0.5625 - 0.25) = 49\times 0.3125 = 15.3125\ \mathrm{J}$$

This is the gain in elastic potential energy of the string.

**Work done in stretching the string $\approx 15.3\ \mathrm{J}$.**
themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics

questions.enonce_markdown:
A car of mass $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ moves along a straight horizontal road. The engine works at a constant rate of $50\ \mathrm{kW}$ against a constant resistance of magnitude $5000\ \mathrm{N}$ to the motion of the car.

Find the maximum speed of the car.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $F$ be the driving force of the engine (along the direction of motion) and $R = 5000\ \mathrm{N}$ the resistance. The power is $P = Fv$, with $P = 50\,000\ \mathrm{W}$ constant.

The speed is maximum when the acceleration is zero, i.e. when the resultant force is zero: $F = R$. Then

$$P = Fv_{\max} = Rv_{\max}\;\Longrightarrow\;v_{\max} = \frac{P}{R} = \frac{50\,000}{5000} = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

**Maximum speed $= 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ ($= 36\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$).**
themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance

questions.enonce_markdown:
A car of mass $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ moves along a straight horizontal road. The engine works at a constant rate of $50\ \mathrm{kW}$ against a constant resistance of magnitude $5000\ \mathrm{N}$ to the motion of the car.

If the speed $v$ of the car is not maximum, show that the acceleration $a$ of the car is given by $a = \dfrac{50 - 5v}{v}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Forces along the road** (positive direction = direction of motion): driving force $F$ forwards, resistance $5000\ \mathrm{N}$ backwards. (The weight and normal reaction are vertical and balance.)

Since the power is constant, $P = Fv$ gives the driving force at speed $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$:

$$F = \frac{P}{v} = \frac{50\,000}{v}\ \mathrm{N}$$

Newton's second law along the road, $F - R = ma$:

$$\frac{50\,000}{v} - 5000 = 1000\,a$$

Dividing by $1000$:

$$a = \frac{50}{v} - 5 = \frac{50 - 5v}{v}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\qquad\blacksquare$$

(Check: $a = 0$ when $v = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the maximum speed of part (a); for $v < 10$ the acceleration is positive.)
themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance
